translation_en: Anas ibn Malik reported that people from Ukl or Uraynah came to the Messenger and found Madinah’s climate unsuitable. He provided milk camels and told them to drink the camels’ urine and milk. This is like Hajjaj ibn Abi Uthman’s report. It adds that their eyes were branded and they were left on the stony plain, asking for water but being denied it. The chain is Harun ibn Abdullah, Sulayman ibn Harb, Hammad ibn Zayd, Ayyub, Abu Raja, Abu Qilabah, and Anas ibn Malik.

Abu Qilabah said that while he was sitting behind Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Umar asked what they knew about the oath procedure. Anbasah mentioned a report from Anas. Abu Qilabah said Anas himself had told him about people who came to the Prophet, and related a similar account. When he finished, Anbasah said, “Glory be to Allah!” Abu Qilabah asked whether he suspected him. Anbasah said no, and added that Anas used to say, “You people of Syria will remain in a good state as long as this man, or someone like him, is among you.”

Anas reported that eight men from Ukl came to the Messenger. This is like the preceding reports, with the addition that their wounds were not cauterized. The report comes through al-Awzai, Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, Abu Qilabah, and Anas. It says eight men from Ukl arrived, with wording like the preceding reports, and adds that their wounds were not cauterized.

Anas said people from Uraynah came, accepted Islam, and pledged allegiance when a fever-like illness was in Madinah. This is similar to the preceding reports. It adds that about twenty young Ansaris were with the Prophet, and he sent them after the group with a tracker. The chain is Harun ibn Abdullah, Malik ibn Ismail, Zuhayr, Simak ibn Harb, Muawiyah ibn Qurrah, and Anas. It says a fever-like illness had struck Madinah and the Prophet sent about twenty young Ansaris with a tracker after the fleeing group.

This is similar to the preceding reports. Hammam’s version says the people were from Uraynah; Said’s says Ukl and Uraynah. The report comes through Hammad, Qatadah, and Anas, and through Abd al-Ala, Said, and Qatadah from Anas. Hammam’s version identifies the people as from Uraynah; Said’s says Ukl and Uraynah.

Anas said the Prophet branded their eyes because they had branded the eyes of the herdsmen. Anas said: “The Prophet branded those men’s eyes only because they had branded the herdsmen’s eyes.” The chain is al-Fadl ibn Sahl, Yahya ibn Ghailan, Yazid ibn Zuray, and Sulayman al-Taymi.

Anas reported that a Jewish man killed a girl for silver ornaments she wore, striking her head with a stone. She was brought to the Prophet while still alive. He asked whether a certain man had killed her. She shook her head no. He asked a second time, and she again shook her head no. He asked a third time, and she indicated yes. The Messenger then killed the man between two stones. The girl was brought to the Prophet still alive. He asked her three times whether a certain man had killed her. She first shook her head no twice, then indicated yes the third time. The chain is Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, Muhammad ibn Bashshar, Muhammad ibn Jafar, Shubah, Hisham ibn Zayd, and Anas.
This is a similar report through Khalid ibn al-Harith and Ibn Idris from Shubah and the same chain. Ibn Idris’s version says the man’s head was crushed between two stones.

Anas reported that a Jewish man killed an Ansari girl for jewelry, threw her into a well, and crushed her head with stones. He was captured and brought to the Messenger, who ordered that he be stoned until he died. The man was seized and brought to the Messenger, who ordered that he be stoned until death. This report is through Abd ibn Humayd, Abd al-Razzaq, Maamar, Ayyub, Abu Qilabah, and Anas.
This is the same report through Muhammad ibn Bakr and Ibn Jurayj from Maamar and Ayyub, with the same chain.

Anas reported that a girl was found with her head crushed between two stones. They asked who had done it, naming several people until they mentioned a Jewish man. She nodded. The Jewish man was seized and confessed. The Messenger ordered that his head be crushed with stones.

Imran ibn Husayn said Yala ibn Munyah—or Ibn Umayyah—was fighting a man. One bit the other, and the man pulled his hand from the biter’s mouth, knocking out one front tooth—or, according to Ibn al-Muthanna, both teeth. They brought their dispute to the Prophet, who said: “Would one of you bite like a stallion? There is no compensation for that.”

This is a similar report through Muhammad ibn Jafar, Shubah, Qatadah, Ata, Ibn Yala, and Yala, from the Prophet. This is the same ruling transmitted by Muhammad ibn Jafar, Shubah, Qatadah, Ata, Ibn Yala, and Yala from the Prophet.

Imran reported that a man bit another man’s arm. When the latter pulled it away, a front tooth fell out. The case was brought to the Prophet, who dismissed the claim and said: “Did you expect him to let you eat his flesh?”

Imran reported that a man bit another man’s hand. When the victim pulled it away, one or both of the biter’s front teeth fell out. He sought judgment from the Messenger, who said: “Should I tell him to leave his hand in your mouth so you can chew it like a stallion? Hold your hand out for him to bite, then pull it away.”

An employer of Yala ibn Munyah was bitten on the arm. When he pulled away, the biter lost a front tooth. The case went to the Prophet, who dismissed the claim and said: “Did you expect him to let you chew it like a stallion?” The report is transmitted through Muadh ibn Hisham, his father, Qatadah, Budayl, Ata ibn Abi Rabah, Safwan ibn Yala, and Yala.

Safwan ibn Yala ibn Umayyah said: “I went on the Tabuk campaign with the Prophet. I had a hired worker who fought with a man. One bit the other’s hand. The bitten man pulled his hand from the biter’s mouth and knocked out one of his front teeth. They came to the Prophet, who dismissed the claim for the tooth.” Yala used to say that campaign was among his most reliable deeds.

This is the same report through Amr ibn Zurarah and Ismail ibn Ibrahim from Ibn Jurayj, with similar wording. Yala said: “I went on the Tabuk expedition with the Prophet, which I considered my most dependable deed. I had a hired worker who fought with a man, and one bit the other’s hand. The man whose hand was bitten pulled it from the biter’s mouth and knocked out one of his front teeth. They came to the Prophet, who dismissed the claim for the tooth.” Safwan explained that Yala had told him which man bit the other. The chain is Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Usamah, Ibn Jurayj, Ata, Safwan ibn Yala ibn Umayyah, and his father.

Anas reported that al-Rubayyi’s sister, Umm Harithah, injured someone. They brought the dispute to the Prophet, who said, “Retaliation, retaliation.” Umm al-Rubayyi said, “Would retaliation be taken from her? By Allah, it will not.” The Prophet said, “Retaliation is prescribed in Allah’s Book.” She continued to object until they accepted blood money. The Messenger then said: “Among Allah’s servants are those who, if they swear by Allah, He fulfills their oath.”

Abdullah reported that the Messenger said: “It is not lawful to take the life of a Muslim who testifies there is no god but Allah and that I am His Messenger, except in one of three cases: a married adulterer, a life for a life, or one who leaves his religion and separates from the community.” Anas reported that al-Rubayyi’s sister, Umm Harithah, injured someone and the dispute was brought to the Prophet. He demanded retaliation. Umm al-Rubayyi objected that the woman would never be subject to retaliation. The Prophet said retaliation was prescribed in Allah’s Book. She continued until they accepted blood money. The Messenger then said that some of Allah’s servants, if they swear by Allah, have their oath fulfilled. The chain is Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, Affan ibn Muslim, Hammad, Thabit, and Anas.

This is the same report through Ibn Numayr, Ibn Abi Umar, Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, and Ali ibn Khashram, all from al-Amash, with the same chain. Abdullah reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “The blood of a Muslim who testifies that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah is not lawful except in one of three cases: a married adulterer, a life for a life, or one who abandons his religion and separates from the community.” The chain is Hafs ibn Ghiyath, Abu Muawiyah, Waki, al-Amash, Abdullah ibn Murrah, Masruq, and Abdullah.

Abdullah said the Messenger stood among them and said: “By Him besides whom there is no god, it is not lawful to take the life of a Muslim who testifies there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger, except in three cases: one who abandons Islam and separates from the community, a married adulterer, or a life for a life.” Al-Amash said he related this to Ibrahim, who told him a similar report from al-Aswad and Aishah.

This is a similar report through Ubayd Allah ibn Musa and Shayban from al-Amash, with both chains. It resembles Sufyan’s report but omits the words “By Him besides whom there is no god.” Abdullah said the Messenger stood among them and swore by Allah, besides whom there is no god, that a Muslim’s life is inviolable except for three people: one who leaves Islam and separates from the community, a married adulterer, and a life for a life. Ahmad was unsure whether the phrase referred to leaving Islam or leaving the community. Al-Amash said Ibrahim reported a similar account from al-Aswad and Aishah.
Abdullah reported that the Messenger said: “No one is killed unjustly without the first son of Adam bearing a share of its blood, because he was the first to establish killing.”

This is the same report through several chains from al-Amash. Jarir and Isa ibn Yunus say, “because he established killing,” omitting “the first.” Abdullah reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “No person is killed unjustly without the first son of Adam bearing a share of the blood, because he was the first to establish killing.” The chain is Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Numayr, Abu Muawiyah, al-Amash, Abdullah ibn Murrah, Masruq, and Abdullah.

Abdullah reported that the Messenger said: “The first matter judged among people on the Day of Resurrection will be cases of bloodshed.” This is the same report through Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah, Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, and Ibn Abi Umar, from Jarir, Isa ibn Yunus, and Sufyan, all through al-Amash. Jarir and Isa say “because he established killing,” without the word “first.”

This is the same report through other chains from al-Amash and Abu Wail. Some versions say “judged,” while others say “settled among people.” Abdullah reported that the Messenger said: “The first matters judged among people on the Day of Resurrection will be bloodshed.” The chains include Waki, al-Amash, Abu Wail, and Abdullah.

Abu Bakrah reported that the Messenger said: “Time has returned to the state it was in when Allah created the heavens and the earth. The year is twelve months, four sacred: three consecutive months, Dhu al-Qadah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and al-Muharram, and Rajab of Mudar, between Jumada and Shaban.” He asked what month it was; they said Allah and His Messenger knew best. He paused, then asked, “Is it not Dhu al-Hijjah?” They said yes. He asked what land it was; they said Allah and His Messenger knew best. He paused, then asked, “Is it not the Sacred City?” They said yes. He asked what day it was; they said Allah and His Messenger knew best. He paused, then asked, “Is it not the Day of Sacrifice?” They said yes. He said, “Your blood, property, and honor are sacred to one another like the sanctity of this day, in this land, in this month. You will meet your Lord and He will ask about your deeds. Do not return after me to disbelief—or error—striking one another’s necks. Let those present convey this to those absent; some who hear it secondhand may understand it better than some who heard it directly.” He then asked, “Have I conveyed the message?” Ibn Habib’s version says “Rajab of Mudar”; Abu Bakr’s says “Do not return after me.”

Abu Bakrah said that day he sat on his camel while someone held its reins. The Messenger asked, “Do you know what day this is?” They said Allah and His Messenger knew best. He paused, then said, “Is it not the Day of Sacrifice?” They said yes. He asked the month; they said Allah and His Messenger knew best. He said, “Is it not Dhu al-Hijjah?” They said yes. He asked the land; they said Allah and His Messenger knew best. He said, “Is it not the Sacred City?” They said yes. He said: “Your blood, property, and honor are sacred to one another like the sanctity of this day, month, and land. Let those present convey this to those absent.” Then he sacrificed two white rams and divided a small flock of sheep among them. The Messenger explained that the calendar had returned to its original order: there are twelve months in the year, four sacred months, three of them consecutive—Dhu al-Qadah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and al-Muharram—and Rajab of Mudar, which falls between Jumada and Shaban. He repeatedly asked what month, land, and day they were in. Each time they answered that Allah and His Messenger knew best. He paused long enough that they thought he might rename it, then confirmed Dhu al-Hijjah, the Sacred City, and the Day of Sacrifice. He declared their blood, property, and honor inviolable, just as that day, land, and month were sacred. He warned them that they would meet their Lord and be asked about their deeds. He told them not to return after him to disbelief or error by striking one another’s necks and ordered those present to convey this message to those absent, since a later listener might understand it better than someone who heard it directly. He asked whether he had conveyed the message. The wording differs slightly: Ibn Habib explicitly says Rajab of Mudar, while Abu Bakr’s version says not to return after him. The transmitters are Abd al-Wahhab al-Thaqafi, Ayyub, Ibn Sirin, Ibn Abi Bakrah, and Abu Bakrah.

This report is transmitted through Nasr ibn Ali, Yazid ibn Zuray, Abdullah ibn Awn, Muhammad ibn Sirin, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakrah, with a similar sermon from the Prophet on the Day of Sacrifice. Abu Bakrah said that on that day he sat on his camel while someone held its reins. The Messenger asked, “Do you know what day this is?” They answered that Allah and His Messenger knew best. He paused until they thought he might use another name, then said, “Is it not the Day of Sacrifice?” They said yes. He asked what month it was, and again they answered that Allah and His Messenger knew best. He said, “Is it not Dhu al-Hijjah?” They said yes. He asked what land it was, and they answered as before. He said, “Is it not the Sacred City?” They said yes. He then declared their blood, property, and honor sacred to one another like that day, month, and land, and told those present to inform those absent. Afterward he turned to two white rams and sacrificed them, then sacrificed a small flock of sheep and divided it among the people. This chain is Nasr ibn Ali, Yazid ibn Zuray, Abdullah ibn Awn, Muhammad ibn Sirin, Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakrah, and his father.
